etymology: American campus slang recorded from the late 1960s, origin uncertain; it became a schoolyard staple of the early 1980s for a socially awkward, weak, or uncool boy, in the same insult family as nerd, dork, and geek. The 1980s teen film fixed the type in the national imagination: the scrawny boy with glasses, eating lunch alone or stuffed in a locker.
biblical_def: A dweeb is the kid who doesn’t fit: too thin, too awkward, too eager, wearing the wrong clothes and laughing a beat too late. In Gen X schools the word was a sorting tool; once a boy was a dweeb, the hallway knew where to put him, and sometimes it put him in a locker. The Christian observation is that God sorts people differently, and He is not on the side of the hallway. When Samuel admired Eliab’s height, the Lord stopped him: "man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart" (1Sa 16:7). "He that despiseth his neighbour sinneth" (Pro 14:21), and the Lord Jesus gave a solemn warning about the small and overlooked: "Take heed that ye despise not one of these little ones" (Mat 18:10). Paul goes further, saying that in the body of Christ the members "which seem to be more feeble, are necessary" (1Co 12:22). And the awkward boy himself needs to hear what God says over him: "I am fearfully and wonderfully made" (Psa 139:14). The hallway’s ranking is not heaven’s. Many a Gen X dweeb grew up to be the engineer, the doctor, or the faithful elder; more to the point, every one of them bore the image of God on the day he was mocked. A father can teach his son two things: never use the word to push someone down, and when you see the boy everyone calls a dweeb, go sit with him. That is what Christ did for us.
webster_summary: Gen X schoolyard insult (campus slang from the late 1960s, origin uncertain) for an awkward, weak, uncool boy; Scripture overturns the hallway’s ranking — the LORD looketh on the heart (1Sa 16:7).
webster_full: DWEEB, n. (Gen X slang, late 1960s campus origin, schoolyard peak early 1980s, United States) A socially awkward, unathletic, or uncool person, usually a boy. "Don’t sit with him, he’s a dweeb."
Derived: dweeby, adj.; dweebish. Origin uncertain.
Insult family: nerd, dork, geek, wimp, loser.
No entry in Webster 1828; the word is 20th-century American slang of uncertain origin.
Decode for parents: the word sorts children by the hallway’s standards; teach yours to sit with the boy who gets called it.
scriptures: But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
He that despiseth his neighbour sinneth: but he that hath mercy on the poor, happy is he.
Take heed that ye despise not one of these little ones; for I say unto you, That in heaven their angels do always behold the face of my Father which is in heaven.
Nay, much more those members of the body, which seem to be more feeble, are necessary:
I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well.
corruption_summary: Dweeb ranks children by looks, strength, and cool; Scripture says the LORD looketh on the heart and that the feeble members are necessary.
corruption_paragraphs: The hallway’s ranking. Every school sorts its children, and Gen X schools sorted hard: jocks, preps, burnouts, and at the bottom the dweebs. The ranking was built on the outward appearance — height, muscle, clothes, ease with girls — exactly the scale God refused when Samuel looked at Eliab (1Sa 16:7). To despise a neighbour on that scale is not merely unkind; Solomon calls it sin (Pro 14:21). The boy at the bottom of that ladder is often the one who most needs to hear that God made him on purpose.

The necessary feeble. Paul’s teaching on the body overturns the hallway: the members "which seem to be more feeble, are necessary" (1Co 12:22), and God gives more honour to the parts that lacked it. Christ Himself had "no form nor comeliness" that men should desire Him (Isa 53:2). A Christian boy who learns to befriend the dweeb is learning the shape of the gospel, which came down to the lowest seat and called us friends.
roots_summary: Late-1960s American campus slang (origin uncertain) → early-1980s schoolyard insult → the nerd / dork / geek family; Scripture: the LORD looketh on the heart (1Sa 16:7).

He that despiseth his neighbour sinneth (Pro 14:21).
Take heed that ye despise not one of these little ones (Mat 18:10).

etymology: From English and Scots geck, a fool or dupe (from Low German / Dutch geck; Shakespeare’s Malvolio complains of being made "the most notorious geck and gull" in Twelfth Night). In the early 20th-century American carnival a geek was the lowest sideshow performer, billed as a "wild man" who did degrading stunts for a crowd, a figure made famous by the novel and film Nightmare Alley (1946, 1947). By mid-century it was a schoolboy insult for an odd or awkward person; in the late 1970s and 1980s, with the personal computer, it took on its Gen X sense — a brilliant, socially awkward enthusiast, the computer geek — and Anthony Michael Hall’s character in Sixteen Candles (1984) is credited simply as "The Geek." The 1990s tech boom turned it into a badge of honor.
biblical_def: A geek began as the lowest act in the carnival and ended as the man who builds the software. In between, Gen X used it for the boy with the pocket protector and the home computer, the one who could program in BASIC but could not talk to girls. By the 1990s the geeks were building the future and the word had become a badge: "I’m a total history geek." The Christian observation is that God made the kind of mind that geeks out, and He gave it something worth searching. "The works of the LORD are great, sought out of all them that have pleasure therein" (Psa 111:2). "It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter" (Pro 25:2). When God built His tabernacle, He filled Bezaleel "with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship" (Exo 31:3), and He gave Daniel and his friends "knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom" (Dan 1:17). Deep focus, love of detail, delight in how things work — these are gifts. The old meaning of the word still has a lesson, too: a geck was a fool, and the apostle gladly wore the name: "We are fools for Christ’s sake" (1Co 4:10). A father can tell his geeky son: your mind is made in the image of a God who delights in detail; use it to study His works, serve His people, and do not be ashamed to look foolish for Christ.
webster_summary: From geck (a fool) through the carnival sideshow to the Gen X computer geek (1980s) — the awkward enthusiast turned badge of honor; Scripture: the works of the LORD are sought out of all them that have pleasure therein (Psa 111:2).
webster_full: GEEK, n. (Gen X slang, 1980s sense, United States) A socially awkward person with intense, often technical, enthusiasms; a computer expert. "Ask the geek in third period to fix it."
Compounds and forms: computer geek, history geek, geek out (to enthuse at length), geeky; reclaimed as a badge of honor in the 1990s tech boom.
Earlier senses: a carnival sideshow "wild man" (early 20th c.); a fool or dupe (geck, 16th c.).
Webster 1828: GECK, n. A dupe.
Decode for parents: a geeky child has a God-given appetite for detail; aim it at the works of the LORD (Psa 111:2).
scriptures: The works of the LORD are great, sought out of all them that have pleasure therein.
Pro 25:2
It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter.
Exo 31:3
And I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship,
Dan 1:17
As for these four children, God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom: and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams.
We are fools for Christ's sake, but ye are wise in Christ; we are weak, but ye are strong; ye are honourable, but we are despised.
corruption_summary: Geek once mocked the odd and the awkward; reclaimed, it names a love of learning that Scripture honors when it is aimed at the works of God.
corruption_paragraphs: From sideshow to badge. The word’s history is a parable. It began with the fool and the carnival "wild man" — a man degraded for a crowd’s amusement — and Gen X hallways used it to push the studious boy to the margins. Then the world discovered it needed him. That reversal is not new: God "hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise" (1Co 1:27), and Paul was content to be counted a fool for Christ’s sake (1Co 4:10).

The temptation of the redeemed word. Now that geek is a badge, it has its own danger: knowledge that puffs up, and a life poured into screens, games, and trivia while the weightier matters wait. Bezaleel’s skill was for the tabernacle (Exo 31:3); Daniel’s learning served a God he prayed to three times a day (Dan 1:17). The best geek is the one who searches out the works of the LORD with pleasure (Psa 111:2) and gives Him the glory.
roots_summary: Low German / Dutch geck (fool) → English geck (Shakespeare) → carnival geek (early 1900s) → schoolboy insult → 1980s computer geek → 1990s badge of honor; Scripture: search out a matter (Pro 25:2).

Late 1970s–1980s: computer geek; "The Geek" of Sixteen Candles (1984)

usage: "My brother’s a total computer geek — he built his own modem."
The works of the LORD are great, sought out of all them that have pleasure therein (Psa 111:2).
We are fools for Christ’s sake (1Co 4:10) — the oldest meaning of geck, worn gladly.

etymology: American slang, origin uncertain; recorded from the 1960s and common in Gen X schoolyards of the late 1970s and 1980s for a socially awkward, foolish, or out-of-step person. Derived dorky (adj.) and the mock-Latin dorkus. By the 1990s it had softened into affectionate teasing ("you’re such a dork") and cheerful self-description ("I’m a total dork about baseball cards").
biblical_def: A dork is the person who does the uncool thing without noticing, or notices and does it anyway: dances badly at the wedding, sings too loud in the car, gets excited about something nobody else cares about. Gen X used the word as a sting, and later as a soft tease between friends. The Christian observation is that the Bible’s most famous dork was a king. When the ark of the LORD came into Jerusalem, King David danced before it with all his might, and his wife watched from the window: she "saw king David leaping and dancing before the LORD; and she despised him in her heart" (2Sa 6:16). Michal thought he had embarrassed himself. David’s answer is the best reply ever given to the charge of dorkiness: "I will yet be more vile than thus, and will be base in mine own sight" (2Sa 6:22). He would rather look foolish before men than hold back before God. Paul says the same: "the foolishness of God is wiser than men" (1Co 1:25), and believers should expect the world to "think it strange that ye run not with them to the same excess of riot" (1Pe 4:4). There is a kind of cool that is really the fear of man. "If I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ" (Gal 1:10). A father can tell his children: do not call people dorks to make yourself look bigger; and if loving God, singing loud in church, or refusing the party makes you look like one, wear it like David — with all your might.
webster_summary: Gen X schoolyard insult (origin uncertain; 1960s onward) for the awkward or out-of-step, softened by the 1990s into affectionate teasing; Scripture’s great dork is David dancing before the LORD (2Sa 6:16, 22).
webster_full: DORK, n. (Gen X slang, 1960s origin, schoolyard peak late 1970s–1980s, United States) A socially awkward, foolish, or out-of-step person. "He wore his gym shorts to the dance — what a dork."
Derived: dorky, adj.; mock-Latin dorkus. Origin uncertain.
Later sense: affectionate tease, or the cheerful self-description of an enthusiast ("a band dork").
No entry in Webster 1828; the word is 20th-century American slang of uncertain origin.
Decode for parents: teach your children not to use it to climb over others, and not to fear it when obedience to God looks uncool.
scriptures: And as the ark of the LORD came into the city of David, Michal Saul's daughter looked through a window, and saw king David leaping and dancing before the LORD; and she despised him in her heart.
And I will yet be more vile than thus, and will be base in mine own sight: and of the maidservants which thou hast spoken of, of them shall I be had in honour.
Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men.
Wherein they think it strange that ye run not with them to the same excess of riot, speaking evil of you:
Gal 1:10
For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ.
corruption_summary: Dork polices the uncool and trains children to fear looking foolish; Scripture shows a king who gladly looked foolish before the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: Cool as fear of man. The word works because everyone dreads being called it. Gen X children learned early that looking eager, earnest, or excited was dangerous, and that the safest posture was a shrug. That dread is the fear of man in a teenage costume. Paul names where it ends: "if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ" (Gal 1:10). A child ruled by the fear of looking dorky will one day be too cool to confess Christ in public.

David’s answer. Michal’s contempt (2Sa 6:16) is the voice of every hallway that ever laughed at an earnest boy. David did not argue that he had looked dignified; he said he would be more vile still (2Sa 6:22). Holy enthusiasm is supposed to look strange to the world (1Pe 4:4), and the foolishness of God is wiser than men (1Co 1:25). The Christian is free to be a dork for God, and free from any need to call anyone else one.
roots_summary: American slang of uncertain origin (1960s) → Gen X schoolyard insult (late 1970s–80s) → 1990s affectionate tease; Scripture: David, more vile still before the LORD (2Sa 6:22).

If I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ (Gal 1:10).

etymology: Air + head, a head with nothing in it but air; American slang recorded from the early 1970s and a Gen X staple of the 1980s for a silly, empty-headed, inattentive person, very often aimed at teenage girls and the Valley Girl type. Compare the older empty-headed, featherbrain, and scatterbrain. (The military airhead, ground seized for landing troops by air, is a separate word.)
biblical_def: An airhead is someone whose head seems to hold nothing but air: she forgets what she was saying, misses the obvious, and drifts through the day on the surface of things. In the 1980s the word was usually thrown at girls, often unfairly, and it stuck to anyone who seemed more interested in hair than in thinking. The Christian observation is that Scripture cares a great deal about what fills the head, and that empty is never neutral. "The heart of him that hath understanding seeketh knowledge: but the mouth of fools feedeth on foolishness" (Pro 15:14). The apostle tells believers to "walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise" (Eph 5:15), and he gives the cure for an empty mind: "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom" (Col 3:16). Then he gives a reading list for the imagination: "whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest … think on these things" (Php 4:8). Our Lord’s parable warns what happens to an empty space: the unclean spirit returns and "findeth it empty, swept, and garnished" (Mat 12:44), and moves in with seven worse. A mind with nothing in it does not stay empty; it fills with whatever the culture pours in. A father can refuse the insult — no child of his is a mere airhead — and still take the warning: fill your daughter’s mind and your son’s with the Word, good books, and real conversation, because heads were made to be full.
webster_summary: American slang (early 1970s, Gen X staple) for an empty-headed, inattentive person, often unfairly aimed at girls; Scripture warns that an empty house does not stay empty (Mat 12:44) and fills the mind with the word of Christ (Col 3:16).
webster_full: AIRHEAD, n. (Gen X slang, early 1970s origin, 1980s peak, United States) A silly, empty-headed, or inattentive person. "She’s sweet, but kind of an airhead."
Compare empty-headed, featherbrain, scatterbrain, ditz; derived airheaded.
Unrelated military sense: an airborne beachhead, ground secured for landing troops by air.
No entry in Webster 1828; the compound is 20th-century American slang.
Decode for parents: do not let the label stick to your child; do take its warning — a mind left empty is filled by whatever the culture pours in.
scriptures: The heart of him that hath understanding seeketh knowledge: but the mouth of fools feedeth on foolishness.
Eph 5:15
See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise,
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
Php 4:8

Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
Then he saith, I will return into my house from whence I came out; and when he is come, he findeth it empty, swept, and garnished.
corruption_summary: Airhead mocks the empty mind, and too often the girl it is aimed at; Scripture warns that an empty mind is never safe and fills it with the word of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: A careless label. The word did real damage in Gen X schools, mostly to girls who were pretty, cheerful, or quiet and were assumed to have nothing inside. Some of them stopped trying to prove otherwise. Calling an image-bearer an airhead is a small act of contempt, and it often says more about the speaker’s pride than about the hearer’s mind. A godly father does not let the label land on his daughter, or on anyone else’s.

Empty is not neutral. Still, the word names a real danger. Our Lord’s parable of the swept house (Mat 12:44) teaches that a cleared-out mind with nothing put in its place is an open invitation. The culture is happy to fill an empty head with songs, screens, and slogans. The Christian answer is to let the word of Christ dwell richly (Col 3:16) and to think on whatever is true, honest, just, and pure (Php 4:8).
roots_summary: Air + head → American slang (early 1970s) → Gen X staple of the 1980s; Scripture: the empty house swept and garnished (Mat 12:44); the word of Christ dwelling richly (Col 3:16).

Biblical mind: seek knowledge (Pro 15:14); think on these things (Php 4:8)

Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom (Col 3:16).
An empty house does not stay empty (Mat 12:44); fill it with what is true (Php 4:8).

etymology: A back-formation from ditzy (also ditsy), "silly, scatterbrained," American slang of the 1970s whose origin is uncertain (perhaps a blend of dizzy and dotty). Ditz as a noun was a 1980s Gen X staple, usually for a flighty, giggly, forgetful young woman, and the type became a stock sitcom character through the decade.
biblical_def: A ditz is scattered: she means well, laughs easily, forgets her keys, starts three things and finishes none, and loses the thread of the conversation halfway through her own sentence. The word is gentler than airhead — often affectionate — but it still says, "Nobody expects much from her." The Christian observation is that Scripture meets the scattered heart with tenderness and a cure. The best biblical picture is Martha, busy and distracted with many things, and the Lord’s gentle words to her: "Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part" (Luk 10:41-42). Scatteredness is often not stupidity but a heart pulled in too many directions. James calls the divided heart unstable: "A double minded man is unstable in all his ways" (Jas 1:8). God is not like that: He "is not the author of confusion, but of peace" (1Co 14:33), and He gives His people focus: "Let thine eyes look right on, and let thine eyelids look straight before thee" (Pro 4:25). The Christian father will not let his daughter be labelled a ditz and written off. He will help her gather her heart around the one thing needful — sitting at the feet of Jesus — and watch how many of the many things fall into place. Scripture’s ideal woman is anything but scattered: "She openeth her mouth with wisdom" (Pro 31:26).
webster_summary: Gen X noun (from 1970s ditzy, origin uncertain) for a flighty, scatterbrained person, usually a young woman; Scripture answers the scattered heart with the one thing needful (Luk 10:42).
webster_full: DITZ, n. (Gen X slang, 1980s, United States) A silly, scatterbrained, forgetful person, usually a young woman. "She’s a total ditz — she showed up for the test a day early."
Back-formation from ditzy / ditsy (1970s), origin uncertain; perhaps dizzy + dotty.
Kin: airhead, space cadet, scatterbrain; a stock sitcom type of the 1980s.
No entry in Webster 1828; the word is 20th-century American slang.
Decode for parents: scatteredness is often a heart pulled too many ways; help your child gather it around the one thing needful.
scriptures: And Jesus answered and said unto her, Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things:
But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her.
Jas 1:8
A double minded man is unstable in all his ways.
For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints.
Pro 4:25
Let thine eyes look right on, and let thine eyelids look straight before thee.
corruption_summary: Ditz writes off a scattered girl as harmless and empty; Scripture sees a heart troubled about many things and calls it to the one thing needful.
corruption_paragraphs: Low expectations. The ditz was a favorite sitcom type because she was easy: pretty, giggly, and never expected to think. Real girls learned the role because it was rewarded. A daughter who discovers that being scattered earns laughs and lets her off the hook may never discover the mind God gave her. The woman of Proverbs 31 is busy with many things, yet she "openeth her mouth with wisdom" (Pro 31:26); no one writes her off.

Many things, one thing. The cure for scatteredness is not a planner but a center. Martha was not a fool; she was distracted, and the Lord did not mock her but called her by name, twice, and pointed her to the one thing needful (Luk 10:41-42). The God who is not the author of confusion (1Co 14:33) gathers a divided heart (Jas 1:8) around Himself, and the eyes learn to look straight on (Pro 4:25).
roots_summary: Perhaps dizzy + dotty → 1970s ditzy → 1980s noun ditz → sitcom stock type; Scripture: Martha, Martha … one thing is needful (Luk 10:41-42).

etymology: From mid-century science fiction: Robert A. Heinlein’s juvenile novel Space Cadet (1948) and the television series Tom Corbett, Space Cadet (1950–55) made the space cadet a boy’s hero. In the 1960s and 1970s counterculture, spaced out described someone dazed (often from drugs), and space cadet became a joke name for such a person. By the 1980s Gen X used it simply for a dreamy, absent-minded, out-of-touch person — someone whose mind is "somewhere out in space."
biblical_def: A space cadet is someone whose mind is elsewhere: he stares out the window in algebra, walks past his own house, and answers a question nobody asked. The phrase began as a hero — the uniformed boy of 1950s science fiction — and ended as a teasing name for the daydreamer. The Christian observation is that Scripture has two things to say, and they pull in opposite directions. First, God wants an alert mind. "Gird up the loins of your mind, be sober" (1Pe 1:13); "Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour" (1Pe 5:8). "Keep thy heart with all diligence" (Pro 4:23). A drifting mind is an unguarded one, and the counterculture’s chemical way of spacing out is no friend to the soul. Second, Scripture does want our minds somewhere else — just not in outer space. "Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth" (Col 3:2). "Our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ" (Php 3:20). The Christian is meant to be a kind of cadet in training for another country, but fully awake in this one, doing his homework and loving his neighbour as a citizen of heaven. A father can tell his dreamy son: your imagination is a gift; tether it, keep watch, and point it at the Lord who is coming back.
webster_summary: From 1950s science fiction (Space Cadet, 1948; Tom Corbett, 1950–55) through 1960s–70s spaced out to the Gen X daydreamer; Scripture says be sober (1Pe 5:8) and set your affection on things above (Col 3:2).
webster_full: SPACE CADET, n. (Gen X slang, 1970s–1980s, United States) A dreamy, absent-minded, out-of-touch person. "Earth to space cadet — the bell rang ten minutes ago."
From Heinlein’s novel Space Cadet (1948) and TV’s Tom Corbett, Space Cadet (1950–55); the joke sense from counterculture spaced out.
Companions: spacey, spaced out, Earth to … (the teasing call to a daydreamer).

Webster 1828: CADET, n. 1. The younger or youngest son. 2. A gentleman who carries arms in a regiment, as a private man, with a view to acquire military skill, and obtain a commission. His service is voluntary, but he receives pay, and thus is distinguished from a volunteer. 3. A young man, in a military school.
Decode for parents: once a drug-culture joke, now a gentle tease for daydreamers; teach a mind that is both alert on earth and set on heaven.
scriptures: Wherefore gird up the loins of your mind, be sober, and hope to the end for the grace that is to be brought unto you at the revelation of Jesus Christ;
Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour:
Pro 4:23
Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.
Col 3:2
Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth.
Php 3:20
For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ:
corruption_summary: Space cadet laughs at the drifting mind, and once at the drugged one; Scripture calls for a mind sober and watchful on earth and set on things above.
corruption_paragraphs: Spaced out. The phrase picked up its joke in the counterculture, where getting "spaced out" was something people did on purpose. That history is worth naming to a child, because the wish to float away from reality is old, and it is never neutral. Peter’s repeated call to be sober (1Pe 1:13; 1Pe 5:8) is not a call to be dull; it is a call to be awake in a world with a roaring lion in it.

The right elsewhere. And yet the Christian is supposed to have his mind partly elsewhere. Paul tells believers to set their affection on things above (Col 3:2) and reminds them that their citizenship is in heaven (Php 3:20). The difference is direction and anchor: the space cadet drifts away from duty; the citizen of heaven looks up for his returning King and so does his earthly duty better. Keep the heart with all diligence (Pro 4:23), and let it look up.
roots_summary: Latin caput → French cadet (younger son, officer in training) → Heinlein’s Space Cadet (1948) → counterculture spaced out → Gen X daydreamer; Scripture: be sober (1Pe 5:8); our conversation is in heaven (Php 3:20).
roots_lines: Latin spatium → space; Latin caput → French cadet — younger son, officer in training
1948 Heinlein novel Space Cadet; 1950–55 TV Tom Corbett, Space Cadet
1960s–70s counterculture: spaced out, dazed; space cadet as a joke
1980s Gen X: a dreamy, absent-minded person; "Earth to …"
Biblical mind: gird up the loins of your mind (1Pe 1:13); set your affection on things above (Col 3:2)
usage: "You put the cereal in the fridge? Okay, space cadet."
Be sober, be vigilant (1Pe 5:8).
For our conversation is in heaven (Php 3:20) — the right kind of elsewhere.

etymology: A run-together spelling of want to be. American slang of the early 1980s (surfers used it for posers who wanted to be taken for the real thing), it went national in 1985 for the teenage girls who copied Madonna’s lace, bangles, and hair — the "Madonna wannabes" — and was soon applied to anyone imitating a group or a star: rapper wannabes, gang wannabes, executive wannabes.
biblical_def: A wannabe is someone trying to be someone else: the girl in the Madonna lace, the suburban boy imitating a rapper, the junior executive copying the boss’s tie. The word is a sneer — it says, "You’re not the real thing, and everyone can tell." The Christian observation is surprising: Scripture does not tell us to stop wanting to be like someone. It tells us whom to want to be like. "Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children" (Eph 5:1). Paul even says, "Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ" (1Co 11:1). Every Christian is meant to be a wannabe in the right direction — a disciple, which means an imitator. The trouble with the Gen X wannabe was not imitation but its object and its motive. The object was a celebrity or a crowd; the motive was approval. Paul names that motive and refuses it: "do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ" (Gal 1:10). He also names the trap of measuring ourselves by the crowd: those "comparing themselves among themselves, are not wise" (2Co 10:12). The world will always press a child to be conformed; the gospel promises something better: "be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind" (Rom 12:2). A father can tell his daughter: don’t be a wannabe of anyone on a poster; be a follower of Christ, and let Him make you more truly yourself than any copy ever could.
webster_summary: Gen X noun (from want to be; national with the "Madonna wannabes" of 1985) for an imitator of a star or crowd; Scripture redirects imitation: Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children (Eph 5:1).
webster_full: WANNABE, n. (Gen X slang, early-to-mid 1980s, United States) One who imitates a star, group, or type in hope of being taken for the real thing. "She’s just a Madonna wannabe."
Also wannabee; used attributively ("a wannabe rock star"). Kin to poser.
Applied widely by the 1990s: gang wannabes, rapper wannabes, executive wannabes.
Webster 1828: WANT, n. 1. Deficiency; defect; the absence of that which is necessary or useful; as a want of power or knowledge for any purpose; want of food and clothing. …
Decode for parents: every child imitates someone; the question is whom — point yours to Christ and to believers who follow Him (1Co 11:1).
scriptures: Eph 5:1
Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children;
Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ.
Gal 1:10
For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ.

For we dare not make ourselves of the number, or compare ourselves with some that commend themselves: but they measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves among themselves, are not wise.
Rom 12:2
And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.
corruption_summary: Wannabe sneers at imitation of the crowd; Scripture redirects the same instinct, calling believers to be followers of God as dear children.
corruption_paragraphs: Imitation for approval. The Madonna wannabes of 1985 were copying a pop star who wore the crucifix as costume jewelry, and they did it to be noticed. That is the double danger of the word: a bad model and an approval-seeking motive. Paul refuses both. He will not please men at the cost of serving Christ (Gal 1:10), and he warns that people who measure themselves against one another are not wise (2Co 10:12). The crowd is a poor mirror.

The right wannabe. The gospel does not abolish imitation; it sanctifies it. Children were made to copy, and God tells them whom: be followers of God, as dear children (Eph 5:1), and follow faithful men as they follow Christ (1Co 11:1). The world conforms; Christ transforms (Rom 12:2). The Christian is not a cheap copy but a growing likeness, and the likeness is real because the Spirit who forms it is real.
roots_summary: Old Norse vanta → English want → spoken wanna be → 1980s wannabe (Madonna wannabes, 1985); Scripture: Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ (1Co 11:1).
roots_lines: Old Norse vanta — to lack → English want — to lack, to desire
Spoken want to be run together as wannabe
Early 1980s: surfers’ name for a poser
1985: the "Madonna wannabes" take it national; later any imitator
Biblical imitation: followers of God as dear children (Eph 5:1); transformed, not conformed (Rom 12:2)
usage: "Look at him with the sunglasses indoors. Total wannabe."
Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children (Eph 5:1).
Be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed (Rom 12:2).

etymology: Short for jockstrap, the athletic supporter; by the 1950s–60s American college slang used jock for the athlete himself. In Gen X high schools of the late 1970s and 1980s it named a social tribe — the letter-jacket athletes at the top of the cafeteria — set against nerds, burnouts, and preps; The Breakfast Club (1985) put "an athlete" among its five types. Compounds: dumb jock, jock culture.
biblical_def: A jock is the athlete as a social type: the letter jacket, the gym-built shoulders, the guy who is cheered on Friday night and runs the hallway on Monday. Gen X high schools were organized around jocks, and the word could be admiring or bitter depending on who said it — with dumb jock always ready for the boy who was all muscle and no mind. The Christian observation is that Scripture honors athletic discipline and refuses athletic idolatry. Paul loved sports metaphors: "So run, that ye may obtain" (1Co 9:24), and "every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible" (1Co 9:25). Training, self-denial, playing by the rules — "he is not crowned, except he strive lawfully" (2Ti 2:5) — are real virtues. But the apostle also puts the body in its place: "bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things" (1Ti 4:8). And God is not impressed by the stat sheet: "He delighteth not in the strength of the horse: he taketh not pleasure in the legs of a man" (Psa 147:10). The tragedy of the high-school jock is the man whose life peaked at seventeen because his strength was his identity. A father can coach his athletic son hard and cheer him loud, and still teach him the better race — to "run with patience the race that is set before us," "looking unto Jesus" (Heb 12:1-2) — and to use his strength to protect the weaker boy, not to rule over him.
webster_summary: Short for jockstrap; 1950s–60s college slang for an athlete and the Gen X high-school tribe of letter-jacket athletes; Scripture honors the disciplined runner (1Co 9:25) but says bodily exercise profiteth little beside godliness (1Ti 4:8).
webster_full: JOCK, n. (Gen X slang, 1950s–60s college origin, high-school tribe of the late 1970s–1980s, United States) An athlete, especially one whose identity and status rest on sports. "The jocks always sit by the window."
Short for jockstrap, the athletic supporter. Compounds: dumb jock, jock culture; the radio jock (from disc jockey) is a separate word.
Gen X cafeteria tribes: jocks, nerds, preps, burnouts; The Breakfast Club (1985) includes "an athlete."
No entry in Webster 1828; the athletic sense is 20th-century American college slang.
Decode for parents: train and cheer your athlete, but do not let a jersey become his identity — strength is for serving the weak.
scriptures: Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain.
And every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible.
And if a man also strive for masteries, yet is he not crowned, except he strive lawfully.
For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come.
He delighteth not in the strength of the horse: he taketh not pleasure in the legs of a man.
corruption_summary: Jock makes athletic strength a social rank and an identity; Scripture honors the disciplined runner but puts bodily exercise beneath godliness.
corruption_paragraphs: Strength as status. In the Gen X cafeteria the jocks were royalty, and royalty is a temptation. The strong boy learns that muscle buys deference, and some never learn anything else. Scripture’s rule for strength runs the other way: "We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak" (Rom 15:1). A jock who protects the dweeb has understood what strength is for; the one who stuffs him in a locker has only borrowed it.

The better crown. Paul honors the athlete’s discipline (1Co 9:25) and the rules of the game (2Ti 2:5), then lifts the eyes to an incorruptible crown. The danger is the man who peaked at seventeen and has been reliving Friday nights ever since, because his worth was in his legs, and God "taketh not pleasure in the legs of a man" (Psa 147:10). Bodily exercise profits a little (1Ti 4:8); godliness profits for ever.
roots_summary: Jockstrap → 1950s–60s college jock, an athlete → Gen X high-school tribe → dumb jock; Scripture: an incorruptible crown (1Co 9:25); godliness profitable unto all things (1Ti 4:8).
roots_lines: Jockstrap — the athletic supporter; clipped to jock
1950s–60s American college slang: jock — an athlete
Late 1970s–1980s high school: the jocks as a social tribe
The Breakfast Club (1985) and the cafeteria map: jocks, nerds, preps, burnouts
Biblical athletics: so run, that ye may obtain (1Co 9:24); bodily exercise profiteth little (1Ti 4:8)
usage: "He’s a jock, but he’s actually nice to everybody."
Every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things (1Co 9:25).
He taketh not pleasure in the legs of a man (Psa 147:10).

etymology: American slang, origin uncertain; recorded from the 1970s and a Gen X schoolyard taunt of the 1980s for a weakling or coward, someone afraid to take a dare. Derived wussy (adj.) and wuss out (to back down). Compare the older sissy and the near-synonym wimp.
biblical_def: A wuss is the boy who won’t jump off the high dive, won’t take the dare, won’t fight after school. Gen X boys used the word to herd one another into risks, and very often the dare was something foolish or sinful — and the boy who said no was the wise one. The Christian observation has two edges. First, Scripture does call men to courage, and it is not soft about it. "Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee" (Jos 1:9). "Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong" (1Co 16:13). "God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind" (2Ti 1:7). Cowardice is a real sin: the fearful head the list in Revelation 21:8. Second, Scripture defines courage differently than the schoolyard does. Real courage is saying no to the dare, standing alone for the truth, and confessing Christ when it costs something. And real strength is not self-made: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness" (2Co 12:9). The strong are told to carry the weak, not taunt them: "We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak" (Rom 15:1). A father should never call his son a wuss, and should teach him never to be one in the way that matters — afraid of the crowd’s laughter more than of the LORD’s displeasure.
webster_summary: Gen X schoolyard taunt (1970s onward, origin uncertain) for a weakling or coward; Scripture calls men to be strong and of a good courage (Jos 1:9) but defines courage as faithfulness, made perfect in weakness (2Co 12:9).
webster_full: WUSS, n. (Gen X slang, 1970s–1980s, United States) A weakling or coward; one who backs down from a dare. "Come on, jump — don’t be a wuss."
Derived wussy, adj.; wuss out, v., to back down. Origin uncertain.
Near-synonyms: wimp, sissy, chicken, scaredy-cat.
No entry in Webster 1828; the word is 20th-century American slang of uncertain origin.
Decode for parents: boys use it to push each other into dares; teach your son that refusing a sinful dare is the brave thing.
scriptures: Jos 1:9
Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.
Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong.
For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.

And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
Rom 15:1
We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves.
corruption_summary: Wuss shames boys into the crowd’s dares; Scripture commands real courage, defines it as faithfulness to God, and tells the strong to bear the weak.
corruption_paragraphs: Courage counterfeited. The schoolyard version of bravery is doing what the group dares you to do. That is not courage; it is the fear of man wearing a brave face. Joseph running from Potiphar’s wife would have been called a wuss; so would Daniel refusing the king’s meat. Scripture’s courage looks like theirs: standing fast in the faith (1Co 16:13), unafraid because the LORD is with you whithersoever you go (Jos 1:9).

Strength in weakness. The gospel also takes the shame out of weakness. Paul gloried in his infirmities because Christ’s strength is made perfect there (2Co 12:9). The truly strong man does not taunt the timid boy; he bears his infirmities (Rom 15:1) and helps him find the spirit of power, love, and a sound mind (2Ti 1:7). A church should be the one place no frightened child is ever called a wuss.
roots_summary: Origin uncertain (American, 1970s) → Gen X taunt wuss, wussy, wuss out → kin to wimp; Scripture: quit you like men, be strong (1Co 16:13); strength made perfect in weakness (2Co 12:9).
roots_lines: Origin uncertain; American slang recorded from the 1970s
1980s schoolyard taunt: wuss — a weakling, a coward
Derived wussy; wuss out — to back down
Near-synonyms: wimp, sissy, chicken
Biblical courage: be strong and of a good courage (Jos 1:9); not the spirit of fear (2Ti 1:7)
usage: "You’re not going to the party? Wuss." "Nope. Not going."
Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid (Jos 1:9).
My strength is made perfect in weakness (2Co 12:9).

etymology: Origin uncertain; perhaps from whimper, and J. Wellington Wimpy, the soft-spoken, hamburger-loving character of E. C. Segar’s Popeye comic strip (from 1931), is often suggested as an influence. American slang by the 1960s for a feeble, timid, ineffectual man; Gen X used wimp and wimp out (to quit from fear) as playground staples of the 1980s, and in 1987 Newsweek applied "the wimp factor" to Vice President George H. W. Bush. Derived wimpy.
biblical_def: A wimp is a man without backbone: he cannot make a decision, will not stand up for anyone, and folds the moment someone pushes. Gen X boys used it on each other in the gym, and in 1987 the national press used it on a vice president. The Christian observation is that Scripture expects strength from men and defines it carefully. David’s charge to Solomon was plain: "be thou strong therefore, and shew thyself a man" (1Ki 2:2). Joab rallied the army: "Be of good courage, and let us play the men for our people, and for the cities of our God" (2Sa 10:12). Paul’s word to the church: "be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might" (Eph 6:10). But the world often mistakes meekness for wimpiness, and Scripture will not allow that confusion. Christ said, "I am meek and lowly in heart" (Mat 11:29) — and the same Jesus made a scourge of cords and drove the money changers from the temple. Meekness is strength under control, not the absence of strength. "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city" (Pro 16:32). The real wimp, in God’s eyes, is not the gentle man but the man who will not lead, will not protect, and will not speak up for the truth because it might cost him. A father can teach his son to be strong in the Lord, gentle with the weak, and immovable where God has spoken — the kind of man the world has never managed to call a wimp.
webster_summary: American slang (1960s, origin uncertain) for a feeble, timid man, a Gen X playground staple; Scripture commands, shew thyself a man (1Ki 2:2), and shows in Christ that meekness is strength under control (Mat 11:29).
webster_full: WIMP, n. (Gen X slang, 1960s origin, 1980s peak, United States) A feeble, timid, or ineffectual person, especially a man. "Don’t be a wimp — tell the coach what happened."
Derived wimpy, adj.; wimp out, v., to back down from fear. Origin uncertain; perhaps whimper; Popeye’s J. Wellington Wimpy (1931) often suggested.
1987: Newsweek’s "wimp factor" cover on George H. W. Bush carries the word into politics.
No entry in Webster 1828; the word is 20th-century American slang of uncertain origin.
Decode for parents: do not let your son confuse meekness with weakness; teach him strength that leads, protects, and rules its own spirit.
scriptures: I go the way of all the earth: be thou strong therefore, and shew thyself a man;
Be of good courage, and let us play the men for our people, and for the cities of our God: and the LORD do that which seemeth him good.
Eph 6:10
Finally, my brethren, be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might.
Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.
He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city.
corruption_summary: Wimp mocks weakness and often mistakes gentleness for it; Scripture calls men to be strong in the Lord and shows in Christ that meekness is strength under rule.
corruption_paragraphs: The confusion of meek and weak. The Gen X culture that coined wimp also tended to treat any gentle man as one. Scripture separates the two. Christ was meek and lowly (Mat 11:29), yet He overturned tables in the temple and set His face toward Jerusalem. He who rules his spirit is better than he who takes a city (Pro 16:32). A man who can hold his temper and his tongue has more strength, not less.

The real wimp. Scripture’s weak man is the passive man: Adam silent beside his wife, Eli who would not restrain his sons, Pilate washing his hands. The charge to Solomon, "shew thyself a man" (1Ki 2:2), was a charge to keep God’s law and lead. Fathers today face the same call: to play the men for our people (2Sa 10:12), strong not in themselves but in the Lord and in the power of His might (Eph 6:10).
roots_summary: Origin uncertain (perhaps whimper; Popeye’s Wimpy, 1931) → 1960s American wimp → 1980s wimp out → 1987 "wimp factor"; Scripture: be strong in the Lord (Eph 6:10); meek and lowly (Mat 11:29).
roots_lines: Origin uncertain; perhaps from whimper
J. Wellington Wimpy of Popeye (1931) often suggested as an influence
1960s American slang: wimp — a feeble, timid man
1980s Gen X: wimp out; 1987 Newsweek "wimp factor"
Biblical manhood: shew thyself a man (1Ki 2:2); he that ruleth his spirit (Pro 16:32)
usage: "He wimped out and didn’t ask her to the dance."
Be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might (Eph 6:10).
I am meek and lowly in heart (Mat 11:29) — meek, never a wimp.

etymology: Dude + the feminine suffix -ette; Southern California surf and skate slang of the early 1980s for a girl or young woman, spread by 1980s teen comedy and used playfully ever since. Dude itself is 1880s American slang for a dandy, later a city man out West ("dude ranch"), and by the 1960s–80s the all-purpose surfer word for "guy." Dudette never became as common as dude; many girls simply took dude for themselves.
biblical_def: A dudette is a female dude: the girl on the surfboard, the friend at the skate park, the sister who can keep up with the boys. The word was coined half as a joke, because the language needed a feminine for dude and found it by adding -ette. Most of the time it is playful and harmless. The Christian observation is that the word quietly records something true: even in slang, people sense that men and women are not interchangeable. "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them" (Gen 1:27). The woman was made as "an help meet" for the man (Gen 2:18) — not a lesser dude, but his counterpart, equal in dignity and different by design. In Christ she shares fully in every blessing: "there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus" (Gal 3:28), which speaks of equal standing before God, not of erasing the difference God made. Scripture’s portrait of womanhood is not the pale shadow of a man: "Strength and honour are her clothing; and she shall rejoice in time to come" (Pro 31:25), and her finest adornment is "the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price" (1Pe 3:4). A father can enjoy his daughter’s tomboy years, cheer her at the skate park, and still teach her the glory of being a woman — not a dude with a suffix, but a daughter of the King, made female on purpose.
webster_summary: Early-1980s Southern California surf slang (dude + -ette) for a girl or young woman; playful and harmless, it quietly records what Scripture teaches — male and female created he them (Gen 1:27).
webster_full: DUDETTE, n. (Gen X slang, early 1980s, Southern California) A girl or young woman; the feminine of dude. "Hey, dudes and dudettes, the waves are up."
From dude + feminine -ette (as in usherette); never as common as dude, which many girls simply adopted.
Dude: 1880s American slang for a dandy; later a city man out West; by the 1960s–80s surf slang for "guy."
No entry in Webster 1828; both dude and dudette post-date the dictionary.
Decode for parents: playful and harmless; a good opening to teach that God made male and female on purpose (Gen 1:27).
scriptures: Gen 1:27
So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.
Gen 2:18
And the LORD God said, It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him.
Gal 3:28
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.
Strength and honour are her clothing; and she shall rejoice in time to come.
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
corruption_summary: Dudette is a harmless joke that hints at a large truth; the danger lies only in a culture that treats a woman as a lesser or interchangeable man.
corruption_paragraphs: A suffix and a truth. Even surfers felt the need for a separate word, and that small instinct agrees with Genesis: male and female created He them (Gen 1:27). The danger is not the playful word but the drift it can ride on: the idea that the best thing a girl can be is one of the guys. God did not make Eve as a second Adam; He made her a help meet for him (Gen 2:18), equal in dignity and different by design.

Strength and honour. Scripture’s woman is neither weak nor merely decorative. Strength and honour are her clothing (Pro 31:25), and her hidden beauty is of great price in God’s sight (1Pe 3:4). In Christ she stands as a full heir of grace (Gal 3:28). A father who delights in his daughter as a daughter, and not as a dude with a suffix, gives her a gift the culture cannot give. She will need that gift most in the years when the world tells her otherwise.
roots_summary: 1880s American dude (a dandy) → Western "dude ranch" → 1960s–80s surf dude → early-1980s dudette; Scripture: male and female created he them (Gen 1:27).
roots_lines: 1880s American dude — a fastidious dandy; origin uncertain
Early 20th c.: a city man out West; the dude ranch
1960s–80s surf and skate slang: dude — guy, friend
Early 1980s Southern California: dudette — dude + feminine -ette
Biblical design: male and female (Gen 1:27); strength and honour are her clothing (Pro 31:25)
usage: "She’s a total dudette — she skated the half-pipe on her first try."
Male and female created he them (Gen 1:27).
Strength and honour are her clothing (Pro 31:25).

etymology: Party + animal, one who parties with animal abandon; American college slang of the late 1970s, popularized in the wake of National Lampoon’s Animal House (1978), whose fraternity of drunken, toga-clad brothers became the model, and a Gen X boast through the 1980s. Compare party hearty and party on.
biblical_def: A party animal is someone who lives for the weekend: first to the keg, last to leave, legendary for what he did and cannot remember. Gen X made it a boast — the title a freshman wanted by Thanksgiving — and Animal House made it look like the best years of a man’s life. The Christian observation is that the phrase is honest about itself. To party like an animal is to set aside what makes us human: reason, restraint, and the image of God. Scripture names that life plainly. "Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness" (Rom 13:13). Peter remembers it as the old life believers have left: "excess of wine, revellings, banquetings" (1Pe 4:3). "Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise" (Pro 20:1). "Be not among winebibbers" (Pro 23:20). Yet the gospel is not against celebration. God throws the greatest feast in Scripture: when the prodigal comes home, the father kills the fatted calf, "and they began to be merry" (Luk 15:24). The prodigal had already tried the world’s party in the far country and ended among the swine; the real celebration began when he came home. A father should be plain with his son that the party-animal life is a lie that ends in shame, and just as plain that Christians know how to feast — with joy, with thanksgiving, and with nothing to regret in the morning.
webster_summary: Late-1970s college slang (after Animal House, 1978) for one who lives for wild, drunken parties; Scripture calls it rioting and drunkenness (Rom 13:13) and offers instead the Father’s feast for the returning son (Luk 15:24).
webster_full: PARTY ANIMAL, n. (Gen X slang, late 1970s–1980s, United States) One who loves wild parties, especially heavy drinking, and is known for it. "Steve? Total party animal — he’s never missed a kegger."
Popularized after National Lampoon’s Animal House (1978); companions party hearty, party on, kegger.
Often a boast; sometimes a warning from friends who have seen where it ends.
Webster 1828: PARTY, n. [Latin pars. See Part.] 1. A number of persons united in opinion or design, in opposition to others in the community. …
Decode for parents: the phrase admits what it is — partying like an animal; name it, and show your children the Christian feast instead.
scriptures: Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying.
For the time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles, when we walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries:
Pro 20:1
Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise.
Be not among winebibbers; among riotous eaters of flesh:
For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found. And they began to be merry.
corruption_summary: Party animal boasts of laying aside reason and restraint for the bottle; Scripture calls it rioting and drunkenness, and offers the Father’s feast for the son who comes home.
corruption_paragraphs: The honest name. Few slang phrases are as candid as this one. The party animal sets aside the very things that distinguish a man from a beast — judgment, self-rule, memory — and calls it fun. Scripture calls it rioting and drunkenness (Rom 13:13) and says the man deceived by strong drink is not wise (Pro 20:1). Animal House played it for laughs; the emergency rooms and broken homes of the generation that copied it tell the rest of the story.

The better feast. Christianity is not a religion of joyless men. Peter calls the old life of revellings "the time past" (1Pe 4:3), not because joy ended but because a better joy began. The prodigal’s far-country party ended among swine; his father’s feast began with a robe and a ring, "and they began to be merry" (Luk 15:24). The church should be the place where a former party animal learns what a real celebration is.

1980s Gen X boast; companions party hearty, kegger
Biblical feasting: not in rioting and drunkenness (Rom 13:13); the Father’s feast (Luk 15:24)
usage: "Freshman year he was a party animal. Sophomore year he was on academic probation."
